assumptions: The opportunity is judged at planning and pre-validation stage; missing sponsor, clinic, conversion, and renewal evidence is treated as uncertainty rather than proof of failure.

The business launches no participant operations unless sponsor deposits cover contracted first-cohort external costs and the named clinic, principal investigator, coordination, privacy, and quality responsibilities are contractually allocated.

Cross-sponsor outputs are limited to derived metrics for which participant, clinic, sponsor, GDPR, and other applicable rights have been affirmatively documented; EHDS is not assumed to provide near-term access, portability, or exclusivity.
The 175000 PLN amount is an unquoted total-project planning estimate rather than founder-funded launch capital, and the founder abandons the attempt if the pre-funding gate is not met.

The initial scope remains one EEG or sleep endpoint for noncompeting European device teams, with the founder focused on analytics and productization within the stated part-time limit while credentialed work is delegated.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A costed protocol and written regulatory route; signed clinic and qualified-role terms; at least two independent sponsors committing deposits around the same endpoint; counsel-validated participant, clinic, and sponsor terms permitting the proposed derived benchmark; and a pilot model showing price, gross margin, acquisition effort, delivery time, renewal intent, and a credible founder-net-worth path.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Amortizing one stable, clinician-labelled reference protocol across noncompeting device teams could convert repeated validation work into sponsor-specific reports plus a compounding derived benchmark. The hard precommitment gates make the insight more disciplined, but shared-cost studies and standardized benchmarking are plausible packaging improvements rather than a demonstrated proprietary insight, and established wearable CROs already operate close to this territory.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: A new device or algorithm version can require credible protocol-based validation, and the presence of multiple specialist wearable CRO offerings supports real spending on the general job. The unproven part is the proposed buying behavior: there is no evidence that two sponsors will align on endpoint and timing, accept governed sharing, or prepay this consortium rather than purchase a conventional private engagement.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Deposits covering external costs before launch improve cash conversion and cap founder downside, while standardized analysis and permitted benchmark reuse could create operating leverage. However, clinic, recruitment, insurance, regulatory, secure-compute, and biostatistics costs are unquoted; sponsor pricing, gross margin, CAC, sales-cycle payback, renewal, and benchmark-licence demand are unknown. The initial model remains a lumpy clinical-services project, and the stated founder-net-worth path is not economically substantiated.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: European EEG and sleep device teams around one endpoint form a clear and operationally focused beachhead, and individual validation projects can be high value. Requiring noncompeting sponsors with the same endpoint and compatible timing materially narrows the reachable pool, while the packet provides no evidence on buyer count, validation frequency, or spend sufficient to show that this first segment is economically meaningful at repeatable scale.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A repeat protocol, Central-European clinical access, and a shared benchmark could support a focused niche position after several successful cohorts. At present, VivoSense, Empatica, TNO, and Delve already advertise overlapping protocol, analytics, regulatory, device, quality, and participant-support capabilities, while this candidate has no exclusive clinic relationship, channel, rights portfolio, corpus, or measured buying advantage from which to dominate the niche.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful reference protocol could support device-version updates, additional sponsors, nearby EEG or sleep endpoints, and eventually other biosensors or geographies. Expansion is only partly reusable: each new endpoint can require a new sponsor cluster, clinical expertise, regulatory analysis, participant consent, operating capacity, and derived-data rights, so adjacency does not automatically inherit the original beachhead's economics or control point.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Contracted reuse rights, accumulated comparable derived metrics, protocol failure modes, and repeat clinic execution could become a useful data and workflow moat. None of those assets or rights exists yet, the lawful reuse boundary may remain narrow, small cohorts may not generate a trusted reference, and better-capitalized incumbent CROs could imitate the consortium format or use their existing sponsor relationships to neutralize it.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Sponsors could gain lower fixed cost per firm, consistent comparisons, and faster reuse of a stable protocol. No cost, speed, accuracy, credibility, or conversion advantage is quantified, and the need to compromise on a shared endpoint plus weaker entrant trust may offset the benefit relative to a private study with an established provider.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Wearable and digital-measure development plus continuing regulatory demand for credible evidence create a relevant backdrop. The timing advantage is not specific or urgent: incumbents are already active, EHDS does not remove current consent, permit, or device-study obligations, and its key secondary-use availability for clinical-study and cohort data is phased well beyond the near-term validation period.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The first sale requires multiple high-trust enterprise buyers to align on one protocol while a clinic and qualified roles also commit on acceptable terms. There is no signed channel, sponsor pipeline, clinic referral mechanism, conversion evidence, or measured sales cycle. Focused founder-led outreach is possible, but simultaneous consortium formation is intrinsically harder to repeat than a bilateral CRO sale and strains the founder's part-time and social-energy constraints.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's neuroscience, EEG, data-science, and AI leverage fit protocol analytics, and the no-launch gates appropriately keep clinical and regulated responsibilities with qualified parties. Execution still requires a principal investigator, clinic coordination, ethics and potentially URPL routing, privacy and quality ownership, participant operations, insurance, robust statistics, and multi-party rights contracts. Those capabilities can be contracted but are relationship-heavy, slow, and difficult to coordinate within a part-time founder model.

highest_value_structural_change: Replace simultaneous two-sponsor formation with a clinic- or association-anchored sequential slot model: secure one repeat clinical protocol, template rights, and a channel partner first, require an anchor sponsor to fund the full base cohort, then sell later device-specific comparisons against the permitted reference. This would preserve the no-unfunded-launch discipline while reducing the multi-buyer synchronization bottleneck and creating a more defensible distribution point.
main_structural_strength: The redesign couples a repeat single-endpoint protocol with sponsor-funded pre-launch gates, limiting founder capital exposure while preserving a plausible route from standardized analysis to a lawfully reusable derived benchmark.
primary_score_limiter: The commercial engine depends on synchronizing at least two sponsors, qualified clinic roles, a protocol-specific regulatory route, and cross-sponsor derived-data rights before any delivery, without an existing channel or demonstrated advantage over established wearable CROs.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: VivoSense, Empatica, TNO, and Delve already market substantial portions of the proposed end-to-end wearable validation stack, directly weakening the claim that this entrant has a sufficiently differentiated or uncontested beachhead.
